title: Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning
abstract: This study investigates whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances feature learning for hard temporal tasks compared to standard weight decay. While prior work examines entropy maximization for weight noise robustness and singular value decay in Bayesian networks, there is no investigation into whether minimizing the spectral entropy of input projections specifically improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the baseline, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. Using a Transformer architecture on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split, we evaluated the intervention across 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. The results did not support the preregistered hypothesis. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0004419 proportion (95% CI [-0.00213, 0.0031], p=0.75) relative to the baseline. The replication cohort showed a contrast of 0.002549 (95% CI [-0.000331, 0.0055], p=0.106). In both cohorts, the confidence intervals included zero and failed to exceed the preregistered margin; the preregistered decision was inconclusive. Negative controls performed comparably to the baseline. These findings indicate that spectral entropy minimization of input projections does not provide a measurable generalization benefit over standard weight decay in this regime. Practitioners should not expect subject-disjoint robustness gains from this specific spectral regularization without further evidence.
introduction:
Deep learning models for time-series classification often struggle to generalize when tested on subjects unseen during training. This subject-disjoint generalization gap is critical for deploying activity recognition systems in real-world settings where user variability introduces distribution shifts that standard independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) validation fails to capture. The mechanistic role of weight geometry in facilitating feature learning versus kernel regime behavior in finite-width networks remains an open problem. Specifically, it is unclear whether constraining the singular value spectrum of input projections encourages the model to select dominant temporal modes rather than distributing energy uniformly, thereby improving robustness to subject variability. Current regularization strategies, such as weight decay, penalize parameter magnitude but do not explicitly constrain the structure of the weight matrix spectrum. Alternative approaches involving entropy regularization have been proposed, yet the literature presents conflicting directives on whether entropy should be maximized or minimized to aid robustness. Some work suggests maximizing entropy of weight noise parameters improves confidence under distribution shift, though recent audits have flagged reproducibility and implementation issues in this area [1]. Conversely, other studies indicate that low-entropy latent variables may hurt out-of-distribution performance, suggesting a complex relationship between spectral structure and generalization [5]. There is no investigation into whether minimizing the spectral entropy of input projections specifically improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. This gap leaves practitioners without clear guidance on whether spectral shaping is a viable tool for edge AI where robustness is critical. This paper reports a preregistered experiment testing whether spectral entropy minimization of input projection weights enhances feature learning for hard temporal tasks compared to standard weight decay. We utilize a calibrated testbed with a subject-disjoint split to ensure the evaluation targets the intended distribution shift. The study employs both primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts to distinguish signal from noise. The contributions of this work are:
- We provide a rigorous test of spectral entropy minimization as a regularization mechanism for subject-disjoint time-series classification. - We report null findings across primary and replication cohorts, clarifying that this specific operator does not exceed standard weight decay under these conditions. - We contextualize these results within the broader literature on entropy regularization and weight geometry, highlighting the need for precise mechanistic understanding before deployment.
related_work:
**Time-Series Generalization and Distribution Shift**
Research on generalization in sequential and structured data highlights significant challenges regarding distribution shifts and model capacity. Time series frequently manifest distribution shifts and non-stationary learning dynamics that pose challenges for out-of-distribution generalization [9]. Theoretical work derives generalization results for autoregressive processes by relating empirical loss to denoising loss, characterizing sample complexity in terms of tokens rather than sequences [10]. However, length generalization remains a key challenge for transformers with limited existing theoretical understanding, often requiring auxiliary tasks to provably guarantee performance on longer sequences [11]. Despite advances in algorithms, research on the theoretical analysis of generalization is still in the early stage, particularly regarding how to reduce dependency on label counts and analyze inductive biases [7]. Furthermore, when training data is not independent and identically distributed, algorithm performances are challenged by catastrophic forgetting, indicating that standard regularization may be insufficient for non-i.i.d. regimes [17]. These works collectively establish that time-series transformers operate in a regime where standard generalization bounds are loose and distribution shift is a primary failure mode. **Entropy and Weight Structure in Regularization**
Parallel work examines the role of entropy and weight structure in regularization and robustness. One line of inquiry investigates whether explicitly maximizing the entropy of multiplicative weight noise parameters during training provides calibrated confidence under distribution shift, though this specific claim carries a retraction notice due to implementation discrepancies [1]. Other studies study the relationship between the entropy of intermediate representations and a model's robustness to distributional shift, finding that removal of low-entropy bits can benefit out-of-distribution performance [5]. In Bayesian contexts, it is argued that the parameter cost of standard networks is often unnecessary when weight matrices exhibit fast singular value decay, proposing low-rank parameterization to capture structured weight correlations [14]. Sharpness-Aware Minimization algorithms improve neural network generalization by steering model parameters away from sharp regions of the training loss landscape, suggesting that landscape geometry matters [2]. Additionally, empirical risk minimization is known to fail in various settings for which uniform convergence does not characterize learning, necessitating regularization principles beyond simple risk minimization [6]. This literature suggests that while weight structure and entropy are relevant to generalization, the direction of the effect (minimization vs. maximization) and the target (weights vs. representations) remain contested. **Projections and Dimensionality Reduction**
Methods involving projections offer alternative perspectives on dimensionality and regularization. Work explores reducing problem sizes using random and data-driven projections to accelerate solving, showing that learning projection matrices from data can lead to significantly higher solution quality than random projection [3]. In image processing, regularization strategies utilize denoising engines as regularization strategies for inverse problems through fixed-point projection, bridging theoretical gaps between denoising and optimization frameworks [12]. These methods demonstrate that projections can be learned or constrained to improve solution quality, yet their application to spectral entropy constraints in transformer input layers for time-series data remains unexplored. This study positions itself against these works by testing whether a specific spectral entropy constraint on input projections yields benefits where standard projections or weight decay do not.
method:
The core intervention in this study is the enforcement of a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights via a regularization term added to the training objective. This operator is designed to test the hypothesis that selecting dominant temporal modes improves feature learning compared to distributing energy uniformly across singular values. The regularization term computes the singular value decomposition (SVD) of the weight matrix at each training step, normalizes the singular values to form a probability distribution, and minimizes their Shannon entropy. By penalizing high entropy, the operator encourages the weight matrix to become effectively low-rank during training, concentrating representational capacity into fewer orthogonal directions. This expression of the hypothesis is chosen because it directly targets the geometry of the input projection, which dictates how raw inertial signals are mapped into the transformer's latent space. If feature learning for hard temporal tasks relies on isolating specific frequency modes or temporal patterns, a low-entropy spectrum should theoretically facilitate this by suppressing noise-like uniform distributions. The comparator, standard weight decay, neutralizes this mechanism by penalizing magnitude without regard for spectral structure. Weight decay shrinks weights uniformly but does not enforce orthogonality or rank constraints, allowing the spectrum to remain flat if the optimization landscape permits. By comparing the proposed condition against this baseline, we isolate the effect of spectral shaping from general parameter norm control. The operator is implemented as an additive term to the loss function, scaled to be comparable in magnitude to the classification loss. This ensures that the spectral constraint influences the optimization trajectory without overwhelming the primary task objective. The SVD computation is performed on the CPU to avoid GPU memory bottlenecks, ensuring the regularization is applied consistently across all seeds. The hypothesis predicts that this structural bias will yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator. Specifically, we predict the intervention will exceed the comparator by a fixed worthwhile margin. This prediction rests on the assumption that subject-disjoint robustness requires invariant features that are best captured by dominant singular vectors rather than distributed representations. The method also includes two negative controls to rule out confounding factors. The first negative control involves a regularization term that matches the computational graph of the proposed condition but does not enforce the spectral constraint, ensuring that any performance change is not due to the overhead of the SVD computation itself. The second negative control involves a fixed noise injection that matches the variance of the proposed condition's updates without the spectral targeting, ruling out effects driven purely by noise injection during training. These controls allow us to attribute any observed differences specifically to the spectral entropy minimization rather than implementation artifacts or stochastic regularization effects. The analysis计划 s to compare the mean held-out classification accuracy across conditions using paired contrasts over seeds, adhering to the preregistered margin for significance.

Operator specification. SpectralEntropyRegularization is applied to input_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Singular value distribution of the weight matrix..
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Singular values sorted descending by SVD routine..
- Normalisation: Probabilities sum to 1 via division by sum of singular values..
- Numerical safeguards: Epsilon 1e-8 added to sum and log argument to prevent division by zero and log(0)..

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve target parameter tensor W (shape [64, 9]).
2. Compute singular values sigma = svd(W, compute_uv=False).
3. Compute sum_sigma = sum(sigma) + 1e-8.
4. Normalize probabilities p = sigma / sum_sigma.
5. Compute entropy H = -sum(p * log(p + 1e-8)).
6. Scale term: in the training objective = 0.01 * H.
7. Return in the training objective to harness for addition to objective.

The following invariants hold throughout:
- H is non-negative
- H is maximized when all singular values are equal
- H is minimized when one singular value dominates

Control arm. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.
experimental_setup: The experimental design utilizes a subject-disjoint split to test whether the intervention improves generalization to unseen users, which a random split would have hidden. In time-series activity recognition, data from the same subject is highly correlated; a random split would leak subject-specific features into the training set, inflating accuracy and masking true robustness failures. By holding out entire subjects, we ensure the metric reflects the model's ability to learn invariant temporal features rather than memorizing individual gait or movement styles. This design choice is critical for the research question, as the hypothesis concerns feature learning for hard temporal tasks under distribution shift. We employ 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds to ensure statistical power and reproducibility. The use of paired seeds across conditions controls for initialization variance, allowing us to attribute differences to the regularization operator rather than random weight initialization. Each condition is paired on one seed, which buys precision in the contrast estimate at the cost of requiring synchronized training runs. The analysis uses bootstrap confidence intervals over these seeds to quantify uncertainty in the mean accuracy estimates. This many seeds are required to detect small effect sizes given the variance inherent in stochastic gradient descent on non-convex landscapes. The first negative control rules out the possibility that the computational graph of the SVD regularization introduces optimization artifacts that mimic regularization benefits. Without this control, any improvement could be attributed to the extra computation time or gradient noise rather than the spectral constraint. The second negative control rules out effects indistinguishable from generic noise injection. If the proposed condition performs similarly to the second negative control, it would suggest the benefit comes from stochasticity rather than spectral structure. The design ensures that only a specific spectral entropy minimization effect would validate the hypothesis. The outcome definition is the number of correct activity predictions divided by the total windows in the official subject-disjoint test split, providing a direct measure of operational performance. Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training. The dataset was downloaded, checksum-verified against its published SHA-256 and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started; the exact archive, checksum, licence and training configuration are given in the appendix.
results: We report the evidence for the primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts separately, stating each preregistered decision. In the primary cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.0004419 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00213, 0.0031], paired randomisation p=0.75, Cohen's dz=0.05). As shown in Figure 1, the 95% confidence interval includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.9053 [0.902, 0.908], compared to 0.9049 [0.901, 0.908] for the baseline. The negative controls performed comparably to the baseline, with means of 0.9049 [0.901, 0.908] for both the first and second negative controls. The preregistered decision was inconclusive, as the contrast did not exceed the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.002549 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.000331, 0.0055], paired randomisation p=0.106, Cohen's dz=0.25). Figure 3 displays the final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds for this cohort. The mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.9087 [0.906, 0.912], compared to 0.9061 [0.902, 0.91] for the baseline. The negative controls again matched the baseline at 0.9061 [0.902, 0.91]. The 95% confidence interval includes zero, and the contrast remains below the preregistered margin. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Training dynamics are visualized in Figure 2 and Figure 4, which show the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition. The curves for the proposed condition and the baseline track closely throughout the 12 epochs, with no divergence suggesting a late-emerging benefit. The negative controls also follow this trajectory, confirming that the regularization term did not alter the optimization path in a meaningful way. The effect sizes (Cohen's dz=0.05 in primary, 0.25 in replication) are small, suggesting that even if a true effect exists, it is likely too small to be practically significant for this task. The results consistently show that spectral entropy minimization does not yield the predicted accuracy gain over standard weight decay in this subject-disjoint setting. Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the independent confirmatory replication was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
discussion: The quantitative findings indicate that enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights does not enhance feature learning for hard temporal tasks compared to standard weight decay. This null result holds across both primary and replication cohorts, with confidence intervals consistently including zero and failing to meet the preregistered worthwhile margin. These results contradict the hypothesis that spectral shaping would facilitate invariant feature learning in this regime. When related back to the reviewed prior work, the findings suggest that the mechanistic role of weight spectra in generalization may be more nuanced than simply minimizing entropy. The results do not confirm the claim that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters generalizes to attention-based architectures, nor do they support the inverse (minimization) [1]. While [1] investigated entropy maximization (now retracted), our work tests minimization; both directions fail to show benefit here. This aligns with work suggesting that low-entropy latent variables can hurt out-of-distribution performance, implying that restricting spectral diversity might limit the model's ability to adapt to subject variability [5]. The finding that standard weight decay performs comparably to the spectral constraint supports the view that simple norm regularization is sufficient for this task, echoing arguments that complex parameter costs are often unnecessary when standard methods suffice [14]. The null outcome extends the understanding of regularization in time-series transformers by demonstrating that projection-specific spectral constraints do not automatically translate to robustness gains. While projections offer alternative perspectives on dimensionality [3], and denoising via projection has shown promise in image processing [12], these benefits do not transfer to input weight spectra in activity recognition. The results also resonate with findings that empirical risk minimization failures require specific regularization principles, but spectral entropy minimization is not the correct principle for this domain [6]. The small effect sizes observed suggest that if spectral geometry matters, it is likely at a different layer (e.g., attention heads) or requires a different entropy formulation than the one tested. Practitioners should prioritize standard regularization over explicit spectral entropy minimization for robustness tasks in this regime. The evidence does not support the computational overhead of SVD-based regularization during training. Future work should investigate whether spectral constraints on value projections or output layers yield different results, as the input layer may not be the bottleneck for subject-disjoint generalization. The consistency between primary and replication cohorts strengthens the reliability of this null finding, reducing the likelihood that it is a false negative due to seed variance.
limitations: This study is limited to the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset and a specific Transformer architecture. The results may not generalize to other time-series domains with different signal characteristics, such as medical monitoring or financial data. The spectral entropy minimization was applied only to the input projection weights; constraints on deeper layers might yield different outcomes. The experiment used a fixed regularization scale; adaptive scaling might reveal benefits not captured here. Additionally, the study focuses on classification accuracy; other metrics such as calibration or uncertainty quantification were not evaluated. The computational cost of SVD during training was managed but remains higher than standard weight decay, which may be prohibitive for very large models. Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). Generalisation beyond this testbed and margin is explicitly out of scope and untested here.
conclusion: This study found that minimizing the spectral entropy of input projection weights does not improve held-out classification accuracy over standard weight decay in subject-disjoint time-series transformers. The preregistered hypothesis was not supported, with inconclusive decisions in both primary and replication cohorts. For someone choosing between these methods, the results indicate no benefit to adopting spectral entropy minimization for this task. Standard weight decay remains the efficient and effective choice. To settle the question next, future work should explore spectral constraints on attention mechanisms or evaluate effects on uncertainty calibration rather than accuracy alone.
appendix:
Executed configuration. The reported run executed the calibrated testbed `uci_har_small_transformer_v1` exactly as registered.
- Data: UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). This is real recorded data, not synthetic or simulated: it was downloaded, checksum-verified and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started.
  - `uci_har_smartphones` — https://archive.ics.uci.edu/static/public/240/human+activity+recognition+using+smartphones.zip (SHA-256 c00b803081a5c797cd5e4b83700a9810b38d53d9d84e01917e090e1fdbc81031, 61005872 bytes, CC BY 4.0)
- Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training.
- Model: PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)).
- Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9).
- Held-out evaluation: the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning.
- Outcome: held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion).

references.title: Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness
references.abstract: [EDITORIAL NOTICE — RETRACTED: this paper carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it. Stated reason: The numerical outputs reported in this paper remain computationally reproducible: an independent re-run from the archived reproducibility bundle reproduced all eight aggregate metrics within tolerance. A post-publication audit of the artifact source found that the executed intervention did not implement the preregistered intervention. The preregistration committed to a multiplicative weight perturbation applied BEFORE the forward pass, an entropy term added to the training OBJECTIVE, and a noise scale learned by BACKPROPAGATION, with held-out evaluation on the clean weights. The experiment har. Its conclusions may not be relied on; cite it only with its status stated.] Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is critical for robust deployment, yet standard deterministic training often fails to provide calibrated confidence under distribution shift. This study investigates whether explicitly maximizing the entropy of multiplicative weight noise parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We preregistered a hypothesis that entropy maximization would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the baseline, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. Using a Transformer architecture on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split, we evaluated the intervention across 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. The results refuted the preregistered hypothesis in both cohorts. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by 0.04805 proportion (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002) relative to the baseline. The replication cohort confirmed this degradation with a contrast of -0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). Negative controls involving entropy minimization and fixed noise performed comparably to the deterministic baseline. These findings indicate that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift and may actively impair performance. Practitioners should prioritize standard regularization over explicit entropy maximization for robustness tasks in this regime.

references.title: Generalization Aware Minimization
references.abstract: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) algorithms have effectively improved neural network generalization by steering model parameters away from sharp regions of the training loss landscape, which tend to generalize poorly. However, the underlying mechanisms of SAM are not fully understood, and recent studies question whether its bias toward flatter regions is why it improves generalization. In this work, we introduce Generalization-Aware Minimization (GAM), a generalized version of SAM that employs multiple perturbation steps instead of SAM's single-step perturbations. This allows GAM to directly guide model parameters toward areas of the landscape that generalize better. We show that the expected true (test) loss landscape is a rescaled version of the observed training loss landscape and demonstrate how GAM's multiple perturbative updates can be designed to optimize this expected true loss. Finally, we present a practical online algorithm that adapts GAM's perturbative steps during training to improve generalization, and we empirically validate its superior performance over SAM on benchmark datasets. We believe GAM sheds light on the generalization improvements of sharpness-based algorithms and can inspire the development of optimizers with even better generalization.

references.title: Generalization Bound and Learning Methods for Data-Driven Projections in Linear Programming
references.abstract:
How to solve high-dimensional linear programs (LPs) efficiently is a fundamental question.
Recently, there has been a surge of interest in reducing LP sizes using *random projections*, which can accelerate solving LPs independently of improving LP solvers. 
This paper explores a new direction of *data-driven projections*, which use projection matrices learned from data instead of random projection matrices.
Given training data of $n$-dimensional LPs, we learn an $n\times k$ projection matrix with $n > k$. 
When addressing a future LP instance, we reduce its dimensionality from $n$ to $k$ via the learned projection matrix, solve the resulting LP to obtain a $k$-dimensional solution, and apply the learned matrix to it to recover an $n$-dimensional solution.

On the theoretical side, a natural question is: how much data is sufficient to ensure the quality of recovered solutions? We address this question based on the framework of *data-driven algorithm design*, which connects the amount of data sufficient for establishing generalization bounds to the *pseudo-dimension* of performance metrics. We obtain an $\tilde{\mathrm{O}}(nk^2)$ upper bound on the pseudo-dimension, where $\tilde{\mathrm{O}}$ compresses logarithmic factors. We also provide an $\Omega(nk)$ lower bound, implying our result is tight up to an $\tilde{\mathrm{O}}(k)$ factor. 

On the practical side, we explore two simple methods for learning projection matrices: PCA- and gradient-based methods. While the former is relatively efficient, the latter can sometimes achieve better solution quality. Experiments demonstrate that learning projection matrices from data is indeed beneficial: it leads to significantly higher solution quality than the existing random projection while greatly reducing the time for solving LPs.

references.title: Generalization Bound of Gradient Flow through Training Trajectory and Data-dependent Kernel
references.abstract: Gradient-based optimization methods have shown remarkable empirical success, yet their theoretical generalization properties remain only partially understood. In this paper, we establish a generalization bound for gradient flow that aligns with the classical Rademacher complexity bounds for kernel methods—specifically those based on the RKHS norm and kernel trace—through a data-dependent kernel called the loss path kernel (LPK). Unlike static kernels such as NTK, the LPK captures the entire training trajectory, adapting to both data and optimization dynamics, leading to tighter and more informative generalization guarantees. Moreover, the bound highlights how the norm of the training loss gradients along the optimization trajectory influences the final generalization performance. The key technical ingredients in our proof combine stability analysis of gradient flow with uniform convergence via Rademacher complexity. Our bound recovers existing kernel regression bounds for overparameterized neural networks and shows the feature learning capability of neural networks compared to kernel methods. Numerical experiments on real-world datasets validate that our bounds correlate well with the true generalization gap.

references.title: Low-Entropy Latent Variables Hurt Out-of-Distribution Performance
references.abstract: We study the relationship between the entropy of intermediate representations and a model's robustness to distributional shift. We train models consisting of two feed-forward networks end-to-end separated by a discrete $n$-bit channel on an unsupervised contrastive learning task. Different masking strategies are applied after training that remove a proportion of low-entropy bits, high-entropy bits, or randomly selected bits, and the effects on performance are compared to the baseline accuracy with no mask. We hypothesize that the entropy of a bit serves as a guide to its usefulness out-of-distribution (OOD). Through experiment on three OOD datasets we demonstrate that the removal of low-entropy bits can notably benefit OOD performance. Conversely, we find that top-entropy masking disproportionately harms performance both in-distribution (InD) and OOD.

references.title: Regularization and Optimal Multiclass Learning
references.abstract: The quintessential learning algorithm of empirical risk minimization (ERM) is known to fail in various settings for which uniform convergence does not characterize learning. Relatedly, the practice of machine learning is rife with considerably richer algorithmic techniques, perhaps the most notable of which is regularization. Nevertheless, no such technique or principle has broken away from the pack to characterize optimal learning in these more general settings. The purpose of this work is to precisely characterize the role of regularization in perhaps the simplest setting for which ERM fails: multiclass learning with arbitrary label sets. Using one-inclusion graphs (OIGs), we exhibit optimal learning algorithms that dovetail with tried-and-true algorithmic principles: Occam’s Razor as embodied by structural risk minimization (SRM), the principle of maximum entropy, and Bayesian inference. We also extract from OIGs a combinatorial sequence we term the Hall complexity, which is the first to characterize a problem’s transductive error rate exactly. Lastly, we introduce a generalization of OIGs and the transductive learning setting to the agnostic case, where we show that optimal orientations of Hamming graphs – judged using nodes’ outdegrees minus a system of node-dependent credits – characterize optimal learners exactly. We demonstrate that an agnostic version of the Hall complexity again characterizes error rates exactly, and exhibit an optimal learner using maximum entropy programs.

references.title: Generalization Analysis for Multi-Label Learning
references.abstract: Despite great advances in algorithms for multi-label learning, research on the theoretical analysis of generalization is still in the early stage. Some recent theoretical results has investigated the generalization performance of multi-label learning under several evaluation metrics, however, how to reduce the dependency on the number of labels, explicitly introduce label correlations, and quantitatively analyze the impact of various inductive biases in the generalization analysis of multi-label learning is still a crucial and open problem. In an attempt to make up for the gap in the generalization theory of multi-label learning, we develop several novel vector-contraction inequalities, which exploit the Lipschitz continuity of loss functions, and derive generalization bounds with a weaker dependency on the number of labels than the state of the art in the case of decoupling the relationship among different components, which serves as theoretical guarantees for the generalization of multi-label learning. In addition, we derive the generalization bound for Macro-Averaged AUC and analyze its relationship with class-imbalance. The mild bounds without strong assumptions explain the good generalization ability of multi-label learning with first-order label correlations and high-order label correlations induced by norm regularizers.

references.title: Minimization of the Training Makespan in Hybrid Federated Split Learning
references.abstract: Parallel Split Learning (SL) allows resource-constrained devices that cannot participate in Federated Learning (FL) to train deep neural networks (NNs) by splitting the NN model into parts. In particular, such devices (clients) may offload the processing task of the largest model part to a computationally powerful helper, and multiple helpers may be employed and work in parallel. In hybrid federated and split learning (HFSL), on the other hand, devices can participate in the training process through any of the two protocols (SL and FL), depending on the system's characteristics. This could considerably reduce the maximum training time over all clients (makespan), especially in highly heterogeneous scenarios. In this paper, we study the joint problem of the training protocol selection, client-helper assignments, and scheduling decisions, to minimize the training makespan. We prove this problem is NP-hard and propose two solution methods: one based on the decomposition of the problem by leveraging its inherent symmetry, and a second fully scalable one. Through numerical evaluations using our testbed's measurements, we build a solution strategy comprising these methods. Moreover, this strategy finds a near-optimal solution and achieves a shorter makespan than the baseline schemes by up to 71%.

references.title: Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Time Series: A Survey
references.abstract: Time series frequently manifest distribution shifts, diverse latent features, and non-stationary learning dynamics, particularly in open and evolving environments. These characteristics pose significant challenges for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. While substantial progress has been made, a systematic synthesis of advancements remains lacking. To address this gap, we present the first comprehensive review of OOD generalization methodologies for time series, organized to delineate the field's evolutionary trajectory and contemporary research landscape. We organize our analysis across three foundational dimensions: data distribution, representation learning, and OOD evaluation. For each dimension, we present several popular algorithms in detail. Furthermore, we highlight key application scenarios, emphasizing their real-world impact. Finally, we identify persistent challenges and propose future research directions. A detailed summary of the methods reviewed for the generalization of OOD in time series can be accessed at https://tsood-generalization.com.

references.title: Generalization Bounds for Autoregressive Processes and In-Context Learning
references.abstract: In this paper, we derive generalization results for next-token risk minimization in autoregressive processes of unbounded order. Our starting point is to relate the empirical loss to the denoising loss, which requires no additional assumptions compared to fixed-order Markovian models. We then show that, under a mixing or rephrasability condition on the data-generating process and ass[redacted]g a stable hypothesis class, the out-of-sample generalization error concentrates around the denoising error. These results characterize sample complexity in terms of the number of tokens, rather than the number of i.i.d. sequences. As a primary application, we interpret in-context learning as a special case of autoregressive prediction and derive sample complexity bounds under similar conditions. Importantly, the properties of individual in-context tasks determine the generalization rates, without requiring assumptions on mixture processes. This perspective suggests that in-context learning can exploit the task decomposition to learn efficiently.

references.title: Length Generalization via Auxiliary Tasks
references.abstract:
_Length generalization_, the ability of sequence models to
  generalize to sequences longer than those encountered during
  training, remains a key challenge for transformers,
  especially in tasks requiring algorithmic reasoning. Existing
  theoretical understanding of length generalization is limited, often providing
  only asymptotic results or focusing on specific problem classes or
  architectural variants, while empirical approaches frequently rely on
  ad hoc and often fragile techniques.

  In this work we introduce a novel framework for analyzing and
  proving length generalization bounds under specified, verifiable assumptions. A key
  outcome of the theory is the identification of a natural set of
  _auxiliary_ tasks, intricately related to the primary task structure,
  such that strong performance on these auxiliary tasks, alongside the
  primary task, provably guarantees length generalization within the framework.  This
  motivates a multi-task training procedure that explicitly optimizes
  performance on both the primary and the identified auxiliary tasks.

  Empirical evaluations on a variety of synthetic benchmarks
  known to be challenging for length generalization, including sequence
  sorting, and reversal, demonstrate that our proposed method yields
  significant improvements in generalization to substantially longer
  sequences.

references.title: Regularization by Denoising via Fixed-Point Projection (RED-PRO)
references.abstract: Inverse problems in image processing are typically cast as optimization tasks, consisting of data-fidelity and stabilizing regularization terms. A recent regularization strategy of great interest utilizes the power of denoising engines. Two such methods are the Plug-and-Play Prior (PnP) and Regularization by Denoising (RED). While both have shown state-of-the-art results in various recovery tasks, their theoretical justification is incomplete. In this paper, we aim to bridge between RED and PnP, enriching the understanding of both frameworks. Towards that end, we reformulate RED as a convex optimization problem utilizing a projection (RED-PRO) onto the fixed-point set of demicontractive denoisers. We offer a simple iterative solution to this problem, by which we show that PnP proximal gradient method is a special case of RED-PRO, while providing guarantees for the convergence of both frameworks to globally optimal solutions. In addition, we present relaxations of RED-PRO that allow for handling denoisers with limited fixed-point sets. Finally, we demonstrate RED-PRO for the tasks of image deblurring and super-resolution, showing improved results with respect to the original RED framework.

references.title: A Watermark for Low-entropy and Unbiased Generation in Large Language Models
references.abstract: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have highlighted the risk of misusing them, raising the need for accurate detection of LLM-generated content. In response, a viable solution is to inject imperceptible identifiers into LLMs, known as watermarks. Previous work demonstrates that unbiased watermarks ensure unforgeability and preserve text quality by maintaining the expectation of the LLM output probability distribution. However, previous unbiased watermarking methods suffer from one or more of the following issues: (1) requiring access to white-box LLMs during detection, (2) incurring long detection time, (3) being not robust against simple watermarking attacks, (4) failing to provide statistical guarantees for the type II error of watermark detection, and (5) being not statistically unbiased for low-entropy scenarios, which hinder their deployment in practice. This study proposes the Sampling One Then Accepting (STA-1) method, a watermark that can address all of these issues. Moreover, we discuss the tradeoff between watermark strength and text quality for unbiased watermarks. We show that in low-entropy scenarios, unbiased watermarks face a tradeoff between watermark strength and the risk of unsatisfactory outputs. Experimental results on both low-entropy and high-entropy datasets demonstrate that STA-1 achieves text quality and watermark strength comparable to existing unbiased watermarks, with a low risk of unsatisfactory outputs. Implementation codes for this study are available online (hidden for peer review).

references.title: Singular Bayesian Neural Networks
references.abstract:
Bayesian neural networks promise calibrated uncertainty but require $O(mn)$ parameters for standard mean-field Gaussian posteriors. We argue this cost is often unnecessary, particularly when weight matrices exhibit fast singular value decay.
By parameterizing weights as $W = AB^{\top}$ with $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times r}$, 
$B \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times r}$, we induce a posterior that is \emph{singular} 
with respect to the Lebesgue measure, concentrating on the rank-$r$ manifold. This 
singularity captures structured weight correlations through shared latent 
factors, geometrically distinct from mean-field's independence assumption. We derive PAC-Bayes generalization bounds whose complexity term scales as $\sqrt{r(m+n)}$ instead of $\sqrt{m n}$, and prove loss bounds that decompose the error into optimization and rank-induced bias using the Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem. We further adapt recent Gaussian complexity bounds for low-rank deterministic networks to Bayesian predictive means. 
Empirically, across MLPs, LSTMs, and Transformers on standard benchmarks, our method achieves competitive predictive performance while using up to $33\times$ fewer parameters than 5-member Deep Ensembles. It substantially improves OOD detection and often improves calibration relative to mean-field and perturbation baselines, while Deep Ensembles can still be stronger on in-distribution likelihood-based metrics.

references.title: Minimization I.I.D. Prophet Inequality via Extreme Value Theory: A Unified Approach
references.abstract: The I.I.D. Prophet Inequality is a fundamental problem where, given $n$ independent random variables $X_1,\dots,X_n$ drawn from a known distribution $\mathcal{D}$, one has to decide at every step $i$ whether to stop and accept $X_i$ or discard it forever and continue. The goal is to maximize or minimize the selected value and compete against the all-knowing prophet. For maximization, a tight constant-competitive guarantee of $\approx 0.745$ is well-known (Correa et al, 2019), whereas minimization is qualitatively different: the optimal constant is distribution-dependent and can be arbitrarily large (Livanos and Mehta, 2024). In this paper, we provide a novel framework via the lens of Extreme Value Theory to analyze optimal threshold algorithms. We show that the competitive ratio for the minimization setting has a closed form described by a function $\Lambda$, which depends only on the extreme value index $\gamma$; in particular, it corresponds to $\Lambda(\gamma)$ for $\gamma \leq 0$. Despite the contrast of maximization and minimization, our framework turns out to be universal and we recover the results of (Kennedy and Kertz, 1991) for maximization as well. Surprisingly, the optimal competitive ratio for maximization is given by the same function $\Lambda(\gamma)$, but for $\gamma \geq 0$. Along the way, we obtain several results on the algorithm and the prophet's objectives from the perspective of extreme value theory, which might be of independent interest. We next study single-threshold algorithms for minimization. Using extreme value theory, we generalize the results of (Livanos and Mehta, 2024) which hold only for special classes of distributions, and obtain poly-logarithmic in $n$ guarantees. Finally, we consider the $k$-multi-unit prophet inequality for minimization and show that there exist constant-competitive single-threshold algorithms when $k \geq \log{n}$.

references.title: Low-Entropy Watermark Detection via Bayes' Rule Derived Detector
references.abstract: Text watermarking, which modify tokens to embed watermark, has proven effective in detecting machine-generated texts. Yet its application to low-entropy texts like code and mathematics presents significant challenges. A fair number of tokens in these texts are hardly modifiable without changing the intended meaning, causing statistical measures to falsely indicate the absence of a watermark. Existing research addresses this issue by rely mainly on a limited number of high-entropy tokens, which are considered flexible for modification, and accurately reflecting watermarks. However, their detection accuracy remains suboptimal, as they neglect strong watermark evidences embedded in low entropy tokens modified through watermarking. To overcome this limitation, we introduce Bayes’ Rule derived Watermark Detector (BRWD), which exploit watermark information from every token, by leveraging the posterior probability of watermark’s presence. We theoretically prove the optimality of our method in terms of detection accuracy, and demonstrate its superiority across various datasets, models, and watermark injection strategies. Notably, our method achieves up to 50% and 70% relative improvements in detection accuracy over the best baselines in code generation and math problem-solving tasks, respectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/cczslp/BRWD.

references.title: Regularization Shortcomings for Continual Learning
references.abstract: In most machine learning algorithms, training data is assumed to be independent and identically distributed (iid). When it is not the case, the algorithm's performances are challenged, leading to the famous phenomenon of catastrophic forgetting. Algorithms dealing with it are gathered in the Continual Learning research field. In this paper, we study the regularization based approaches to continual learning and show that those approaches can not learn to discriminate classes from different tasks in an elemental continual benchmark: the class-incremental scenario. We make theoretical reasoning to prove this shortcoming and illustrate it with examples and experiments. Moreover, we show that it can have some important consequences on continual multi-tasks reinforcement learning or in pre-trained models used for continual learning. We believe that highlighting and understanding the shortcomings of regularization strategies will help us to use them more efficiently.
